notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp1207.tmp1207.opp-lat: Printed page numbers (1183–1286) and footnote letters have been omitted. Line 2: 'Ideoque libere non audemus cum possimus' seems defective (perhaps a verb such as 'tacere' has dropped out); rendered with a bracketed supplement. 'Quomodo igitur' read as 'Quoniam igitur'. Line 4: 'cancellarius prior' rendered 'chief chancellor'; the office is uncertain. Line 6: in the Ecclus. 34:16 quotation the text ends abruptly ('quoniam ipse est'); the Vulgate continues 'spes eius', which is supplied in brackets. Line 5: the Psalm is cited as Ps. 50 (Vulgate numbering). Line 7: 'camera' taken as the vaulted ceiling (of the church); the sentence 'hanc verecundiam ... praesagiebat' is grammatically loose.

Line 9: 'Alano' (with footnote mark a) is taken as the monastery's name (Alanum/Attanum, later Saint-Yrieix); the form is uncertain. The sentence 'quae vero post conversionem vita acta sit...' breaks off in the edition. 'Multitudo etiam pau- eum' is defective; read as 'pauperum [ad] eum'. 'Otiositas inimica est animae' is not Pauline (it is from the Rule of Benedict) though the text attributes it to the Apostle. Line 11: 'agnitis qui secum ... adessent' is obscure; rendered loosely. The relation of 'de fonte' (the stones taken 'from the spring') to the earlier stones from the place of execution is unclear. Line 12: 'aerem furarent, dum pavescunt' is probably corrupt (perhaps 'furerent'/'pavescerent'); translated tentatively. 'Noniaco' (Noniacum) not securely identified (perhaps Nexon). Line 1 (VI): the scan's 'lilium' is read as filium, 'son'.

Line 15: 'illiuiret' read as 'illineret' (smeared). Line 16: the opening sentence is obscure ('they raise themselves… [agi]'), translated literally. Line 18: 'Anteslio' read as 'Antestio' (Duke Antestius); 'domnum' read as 'domum' (house); the Bessa passage ('crurum tendit in pagina, nervi laxantur in organa') appears corrupt and is rendered by likely sense. Line 17: 'ledit' read as 'redit'. Line 23: 'basium suarum… vestigiis' taken as 'the soles (bases) of his feet'. Line 27: 'ut a Justo' read as 'ut a justo' (by the just man); 'famula' as 'famulo'.

XXIII: the final sentence ('ut donum a Deo perceptum ... semper sollicita') lacks a main verb and appears incomplete or corrupt; translated as it stands. XXIV: the quotation 'Colloquia mala corrumpunt bonos mores' is ascribed to Solomon but is from 1 Cor. 15:33 (Paul, quoting Menander). Catuliacum is probably Saint-Denis (Catulliacum) near Paris; Brinnacum is probably the royal villa of Berny-Rivière (Brennacum). The king, unnamed, is probably Chilperic I, whose sons died in the dysentery epidemic of 580. 'Ecrli. III, 33' read as Ecclus. 3:33. In XXV 'hinere' read as 'itinere'; 'laedio' as 'taedio' (sickness).

34: 'allevans eum supra vehiculum... regimine ducitur alieno' is awkward; the sense seems to be that Aredius gave up his own carriage and Constantine was driven by another. 35: the Luke reference is printed as XII, 51 (read 31). 'Argentomao' is taken as Argentomagus (Argenton), which is uncertain, and it is odd that it recurs in 36. 29: 'Moeno' is unidentified. The final clause of 29 is grammatically incomplete; the sense is supplied. 30: the opening sentence ('Lemovicum populus ... formidantes moenia rumpere') is garbled, and the translation is approximate. The prophecy appears to refer to the wars around Sigibert, Chilperic and Theodebert. 31: 'sauciorum' read as 'sanctorum'. The sentence 'unicum habens filium' lacks a main verb, and the opening sentence of 31 is obscure.

Line 41: 'nens' after 'amplexusque per singulos' is evidently a scanning fragment (perhaps of 'osculans' or 'flens'); rendered tentatively as '[kissing them?]'. 'ix Kalendas Septembris' is 24 August. 'Astidius' is not otherwise identified. 'velitis' is supplied by the edition. Line 42: the printed reference 'Matth. XIV, 21' should be Matt. 25:21; 'p ontificis' read as 'pontificis', 'Inrbarum' as 'turbarum'. 'ibidem... ubi corpus sacrum jacebat' is ambiguous as to whether the body lay at St Julian's or in the cell.

35: 'statim horarum solvuntur spatia' is obscure; rendered as the release of the halted journey. The sentence beginning 'Praefatus namque Baudenus, cum antequam spiritu perturbaretur' is syntactically garbled. 37: the opening sentence about a woman seems unconnected to what follows; the text may be defective here. 38: 'Ambiacini' unidentified; 'agrum publicum' taken as 'public road' (perhaps 'public field'). 40: 'a frigoribus' taken as fevers (chills); 'nos ambigimus nosse' read as 'non ambigimus'. Ricomagus and Ambiacinum not securely identified.

The first line is the editor's note, not part of the testament. Line 52: the opening sentence seems defective. 'judicantes constituimus ita ut per praepositum' is probably a corruption of something like 'heredem constituimus'. The clause on the monastery is also syntactically broken, so its rendering is approximate. Line 53: 'ina sancia basilica' is read as 'tua sancta basilica'. Line 56: 'carrae' is unclear; it is perhaps a measure or a cart-load, perhaps a payment in wax ('cerae'). 'culogias' is read as 'eulogias'. 'exenio' is read as 'xenio' (a gift). The names Griciensis, Exidolium, Gaudomarum and Eustriacum are not identified. 'Issaudone' is taken as Issoudun.

58: 'ipsorum merres' read as 'ipsorum merces ... liberet'; 'liberei' taken as 'liberet'. 59: the description of the crown and cross ('mimitatae', 'gemmulenas') is garbled; read as 'minutatae' (small) and 'gemmulas'. 'linitam' taken as 'limbatam' (bordered). 'dramioserico' is obscure, perhaps a half-silk fabric. 'profedatam' (Al. 'prosericam') is unexplained. The syntax of the closing sentence is disordered. 61: the syntax is confused, with 'Fexitoialo' unidentified and 'Vosidensibus' presumably Vigeois; the sense of the second clause is uncertain. 63: 'ALSTIDIUS' rendered as Astidius following the glossary. In 63 the first name should read 'AREDIUS'.

nodes.text: THE LIFE OF SAINT AREDIUS, ABBOT.
(Brought to light by Dom J. Mabillon from an old manuscript codex of Saint Gall.)
IN THE NAME OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST, HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE OF SAINT GREGORY, BISHOP OF TOURS, ON THE LIFE OF THE BLESSED AREDIUS, ABBOT OF LIMOGES.

I. Whenever we tell the deeds of the saints, and fix our minds on their acts and examples, we also desire to be their imitators, so that we may not be held caught in a snare in the hardship of this exile. We are lit by grace from above only so far as we are able, with a humbled heart, to climb to the heights in the contemplation of God. And therefore we do not dare [to hold back] freely, when we are able, from setting out to the people, even in slender speech, a story for their edification: especially since we are urged by apostolic authority to record some things about the life and miracles of the saints, as it is written: Let us praise glorious men, who conquered the kingdoms of the world, that their memory may be in blessing, and their name may remain for ever (Ecclus. 44:1); and this: The memory of the saints [is kept] with praises (Prov. 10:7). So when, in the yearly cycle, we celebrate the feasts of the saints, we ought to recite something from their deeds for the edification of the Christians who gather in the praises of Christ. Since, then, the miracles of almost all the confessors, and the many victories of the martyrs, are already set down in written records, we have now tried, according to the measure of our talent, to put together this little book, however slight, in which, with the help of Christ's grace, we take care to set out the birth, the life, and also the glorious death of the holy and most blessed confessor Aredius, so that he whose life is with Christ may have his memory celebrated with glory in the world. For our holy fathers strove to love nothing in the world, so that they might love their neighbours lawfully and perfectly, so that, bound together in one charity, they might be made co-heirs and sharers with Christ. Many indeed from earliest childhood, some in adolescence or in youth, many in old age, serving as soldiers, have striven to cling to the Lord: so that those who once endured the temptations of the world might at some time return to Christ without stain. For the example of a good work done with simple vigour edifies more than much preaching swollen with vainglory. And the excellent preacher, the Teacher of the Gentiles, bears witness, saying: God has chosen the foolish things of the world, to confound the strong (1 Cor. 1:27); and this: The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God (1 Cor. 3:19). The elect, then, are not lifted up by the world's prosperity, so that after the triumph they may be able to take hold of the crown. For if we consider what and how great things are promised us in heaven, the things seen on earth grow worthless in the mind.

II. So the most blessed Aredius, born of a noble family in the province of Aquitaine in Further Gaul, which faces the western region, was a native of the city of Limoges, so that he might be a lamp to all the faithful, by the Lord's gift to his soldiers. His father was called by the name Jucundus, and his mother the blessed Pelagia. Their life bears witness that they were devout, so that, imitating the example of Zechariah and Elizabeth (Luke 1:6), except that John was not among them, they walked in the commandments of God, so as to be without reproach. So Aredius was born and brought up in the right faith; then, steeped in the catholic religion by Christian parents, already passing beyond the years of boyhood, he spent the age of adolescence with great diligence. When his parents saw that their son in adolescence had taken the path of salvation and was adorned with zeal for religion, they handed him over to be educated in letters. He was soon so lit by divine grace that many marvelled at the eloquence in his words, for his sweet speech glowed for all from his honeyed mouth. Bearing an old man's heart, he gave his mind to no pleasure, so that he might not be caught by the hardship of the world and held bound.

III. Meanwhile he was entrusted to the most excellent king Theodebert, to be trained by him in the learning of the palace. So Aredius found favour before the Lord and before the king, and he was well spoken of by all, so much so that he stood as chief chancellor in the king's presence; and his honour grew with great favour from day to day; approved on every side, he flourished in the court; he was held by [the king] in such intimacy that his great good fortune bred hatred in very many. For he hated pride and loved truth: but the good plainly admired him. And so he unfailingly pursued charity, gentleness and humility. For he loved the Lord with all his heart, and with all his soul, and with all his mind. He was also serene in countenance, calm in manner: he always showed good works more in deeds than in words, always committing his hope to Christ, devoting himself often to prayer, and putting nothing before the love of Christ, and his mind was always meditating on the heavenly commands.

IV. When these things had happened, not long afterwards, when he had now reached manhood, desiring to present himself to the Lord as a sanctified vessel, and fearing the dreadful judgements to come, lest any sins should darken his breast, he confessed all the acts of his youth before the most blessed man, Bishop Nicetius. Then, admonished meanwhile by God through the aforesaid Nicetius, bishop of the city of Trier, fleeing the pomp of the world, turning aside from the delights of the world, the vain superstitions of the royal palace, and the undisciplined gossip of his companions, he placed himself under the strictness of a rule, to contemplate the palm of the heavenly fatherland; and so, imposing a harsh penance on himself, he began manfully to resist the struggle of the flesh with fervour of spirit. For he set before himself, against the present burnings of the flesh, the fires of the punishment to come: in labours, that is, according to the Apostle, in vigils, in fasts, in chastity, in sweetness, in much patience, and in unfeigned charity (2 Cor. 6:6). So he prayed to the Lord for heavenly gifts, he besought Christ day and night: he denied himself his fill of bread, so that he might earn the heavenly bread. His face grew pale with fasting, and his body withered, very dry; but his mind burned with desire for eternal things. Always looking to the end of the present life, he dreaded the Lord's sentence to come and his fearful judgements, knowing that it is written: Blessed is the man who is always fearful (Prov. 28:14); and also what was said by Job: For I always feared the Lord as waves swelling over me (Job 31:23); and that saying of the Apostle: Work out your salvation with fear and trembling (Phil. 2:12). For at night he lay before the face of God, beating his breast with his hands, wetting his cheeks with tears, eyes raised to heaven, ever looking to him whom he feared he had perhaps offended by sinning even in the smallest things, and with tears he earnestly prayed these words in the voice of David: Against you alone have I sinned; have mercy on me, Lord, according to your great mercy (Ps. 50:6, 3). And he was always striving towards what the Apostle said: Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what the Lord has prepared for those who love him (1 Cor. 2:9).

So, meditating on these things, the more he advanced, the more he was humbled, according to what the Truth says in the Gospel: He who humbles himself will be exalted, and he who exalts himself will be humbled (Luke 18:14). The more he was humbled, the more he advanced; and so also, as great as his sorrow was, so great his pardon became. O deep kindness of the Lord! O simple penance! And by frequent fasting he obtained from the Lord the mercy he asked for. Of such indeed the Lord says through the prophet: I gave him fear, and he feared me, and trembled before the face of my name (Mal. 2:5). Hence again it is written: He who fears the Lord will tremble at nothing, and will not be afraid, for he himself is [his hope] (Ecclus. 34:16). And again: The fear of the Lord drives out sin (Ecclus. 1:27). Meanwhile he besought the Lord with full vigour that his penance might be accepted before Christ. Then, initiated in these arms, binding himself more tightly in the service of Christ, he shone according to the rule of the Church.

V. One day, while he was keeping the course of a most pure conscience, a dove came gliding down from the vaulted ceiling and, settling on his head, went along with him as his companion through the street, and the man of God Aredius could not drive it from him until he entered his bishop's cell. When the day declined towards evening, it went back the way it had come. In the morning, when the clergy were already returning to the church, it came down on his head as it had done before. As the dove did not cease from this for thirty days, as he himself said in private, the man of God bore this embarrassment, [and] he foresaw that heavenly grace had been given, so that it might be plainly understood that even then, by divine bounty, the Spirit would once for all descend upon him. Hence the Truth bears witness to the disciples, saying: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him; and we will come to him, and make our dwelling with him (John 14:23); for it was fitting that, since he had kept innocence of mind, the visitation of the Holy Spirit should be with him.

VI. Then, after hearing of his father's death, the most blessed man returned to Limoges to console his mother. So the blessed Pelagia, having changed her secular dress, put on the garment of a nun, became a religious in the love of God, and urged her son, well converted, on towards the reward of God. Soon the blessed man sought the wilderness, and, shutting himself away in a hollow rock, there he prayed to the Lord day and night without ceasing, and strove continually to drive back the invisible enemy with prayers and entreaties, fighting with his mouth, not with a sword; with entreaties, not with iron; with prayers, not with a spear. At all hours and at every moment he begged for God's protection, so that after the labour of the world he might worthily attain the prize. When he had been there for some days with great abstinence, his mother, hearing of this, threw herself at her son's feet and asked him to come out from there, so that he might build a monastery cell, where she could readily see him, on pleasant estates.

Then the man of God Aredius found a pleasant place, about three miles from that rock from which he had returned, and there he began with great diligence to build a monastery cell, which was named the monastery of Alanum. And while he was there intent on prayer and devoted to reading, to which he gave his time, his venerable mother, labouring in the fields, sought food for the body; but what life was led after [her] conversion... Then the blessed man grew more and more powerful in vigils and fasts, in prayers and in charity. And his fame began to spread, and religious men, strangers and monks, flocked to him from every side. A multitude of the poor also [came to] him, so much so that, however many poor people flocked to him, none went away from him empty. What more [need be said]? Whatever he had from the property of his noble parents he distributed entirely to the poor and to monasteries, especially to the church of the blessed Martin of Tours and of Saint Hilary of Poitiers, and throughout various churches, and also to his own monastery he gave all his property; and the gold and silver he scattered among the poor, knowing the Apostle's precept: Having food and clothing, with these we are content (1 Tim. 6:8); and: Those who wish to become rich in this world fall into temptation and the snare of the devil (1 Tim. 6:9); and: many useless and harmful desires, which plunge a man into ruin and perdition (ibid.). For he considered what is written: Give alms, and all things are clean for you (Luke 11:41). And the Truth says: He will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life (Matt. 19:29). And elsewhere it is written: Almsgiving frees from death; and whoever has done it will not go into darkness (Tob. 12:9). These things he fulfilled daily: always generous in almsgiving, diligent in vigils, devout in prayer, deep in humility, perfect in charity. He never indulged in idleness; he was always either giving his time to reading, or carrying out the work of Christ, or certainly doing some work with his hands, or else copying sacred books. Above all he had resolved to distribute to the neighbouring dioceses sacred books which he had written with his own hands, remembering what the Apostle said, that Idleness is the enemy of the soul. At these things, then, he never ceased at any time. Now since he had already built the monastery cell, by which he had completed the work he began, it is necessary that, with Christ's help, we should be able to set out something of his miracles. As the servant of God devoted himself to almsgiving, vigils and prayers, we shall gladly make public the miracles that deserve to be proclaimed: of these many, we intend to tell a few very briefly.

VII. It happened that, when the man of God was making a journey to the Auvergne, as night fell he could find no water by which to settle down for a stay. And when his attendants searched here and there and had not found any, then Aredius fixed his staff in the sand. When it was drawn out, an abundant spring leapt up from the hole in the ground, so that the streams of flowing water were sufficient, and afterwards irrigated so much that cattle drank there. Thus this man was great in miracles, and bore the figure of Moses, who by striking the rock gave water to the people in the wilderness.

Then he set to work and chose companions for his journey, whom their religion made distinguished. Having gathered the company, he asked for the support of all their prayers, that the giver of mercy might grant comfort for the coming journey; and so with them, under Christ's guidance, he went to the place where the holy limbs of the holy martyr of God Julian had been buried, having recognised those who were to be with him by the will of the merciful Judge. When they had reached that place, he asked that he himself might be granted relics of the holy martyr, with a devout mind. But the keeper of the basilica of the most blessed martyr refused him his request. Staying there a little while, seeking and finding nothing at all, he went on from there and came to the place where the venerable martyr had been beheaded by the persecutors, long ages before, and with the fullest devotion he took from that same place some very small stones, which is commonly called sand, and gladly put them in the chrismarium which he wore round his neck, in place of sacred relics of the holy martyr. And when he began to return from that province, so great a multitude of those who were troubled by evil spirits followed his footsteps with loud cries that scarcely could so many names be written down. So the fame of the blessed man reached the ears of the bishop of that city, who at once followed the holy man's footsteps with his people, and soon, throwing himself at his feet, began to ask him to come back at last to the tomb of the holy martyr and carry away his sacred relics. Then he said: This gift which almighty God has granted me, I shall go on with it, and with him accompanying me I shall proceed. For the Lord, Creator of all, deigned to show two miracles of power in that same place. When the man of God opened his chrismarium, he found various precious stones from the stones which he had taken from the spring, so that the wonderful power of the holy martyr might be declared throughout various regions of the earth, and the faith of the man of God might be proved and shown to many. And when he deposited the sacred gift with great joy at this place, where the man of God had built an oratory, there too almighty God deigned to display many signs and wonders.

VIII. Nor should what was granted to the servant of Christ be passed over. One day, while he was travelling on the road he had taken, a whirlwind blew, and such rain raged around Aredius that the downpour flowed in streams, yet not a single drop wetted the company itself and his attendants: for the storm was divided, the whirlwind turned elsewhere, and the clouds themselves [seemed to] steal the air, as though they feared the traveller. If, then, sea and winds obeyed the Creator of all amid the waves, and there was a great calm, he also commanded this power to be shown by his faithful one in the sight of all. At one time, when the crops had armed their ears for ripeness, and, weighed down, were already asking to be reaped by the farmer, an enormous rain burst out, so that no one could gather the harvest, and the grains hidden in their ears began to sprout. Meanwhile this was put to him by the people; as intercessor he kept vigils. So on the next day, taking the relics of the saints, fittingly and reverently covered with a small silk cloth, the deacons in white went out in procession; the people cried out against the onslaught of the storms. To them the holy man answered: He who ordered water to be created is able to calm this rain. Then as soon as they went out from the church, suddenly the clouds were cut away, the sun was brought back in its brightness, the calm of the sky was restored to the world, the farmer was drawn to his work, and the reaper was invited by the harvest to gather the sheaves. Nor should what was done in a similar case be passed over. While he was building an oratory in honour of the blessed martyr Julian at his farmstead at Noniacum, and a heavy rain rushed in, as he recited the Lord's Prayer the storm turned aside its onslaught, the tempest drove back the whirlwind, the rain went away, and not a falling drop touched the place or the holy man Aredius.

IX. Let this be added to the page, by which the miracles of these deeds increase. One day, while the same holy man was praying in the oratory, a certain Arctardus, a young man, son of Nivardus, was carried in lifeless and laid by his parents before the holy altar in the oratory of the blessed martyr Julian. He was asked [to pray] that he might be restored to life by the Lord. Then the most reverend man, moved indeed by compassion, with a flood of tears, looking to heaven, besought the Lord. Then he called the little boy, but the body lay lifeless. When about an hour had passed, the boy was roused, opened his closed eyes, and, come back to life, began to be able to speak. Thus the faithful soldier was strong in such great powers and girded with divine grace, so that, just as the Creator of all things raised the widow's young son from his bier and gave him back unharmed to his mother, so the man of God Aredius was able by his prayers to obtain from the Lord that the young man was brought back to life.

A certain woman with a great wound on her face came to Saint Aredius, begging to be healed. Then, when she had been signed with the banner of the cross, at once, with the people standing around, the swelling of the wound opened, and something like a stone, the size of a small nut, came out of it. And she returned home healed without delay.

X. Let there be added to the work a deed joined to these mysteries. A certain son of Dulcissimus, Ingratius by name, lying on his bed, already set out for burial by his father, was so swollen with a tumour that his eyes had been taken away within him. Then the man of the Lord Aredius, having offered a prayer for him, anointed his eyes with blessed oil; and when he smeared them in faith, at once whatever sickness there had been fled at the touch of the ointment.

XI. While they raise themselves as far as they can towards the advancement of the holy man and towards the high contemplation of God, it must be believed that they are [moved] by God. At one time, coming to the city of Limoges out of compassion, he heard that a number of men recently condemned by sentence of death were being held in chains in the prison. So Aredius, mindful of the word of the Lord who says: I was in prison and you came to me (Matt. 25:36); and: As long as you did it to one of the least of mine, you did it to me (ibid., 40), considered whether he might in some way free them. And when he had approached the prison to seek out the condemned, at once, by divine will, as if by the great blow of someone striking, the bolts were broken, the hinges shattered, the doors of the prison thrown open, and all the chains of the fettered men loosed. That same night something like the brightness of the sun appeared within, and light shone out in the darkness; the guards were overcome by sleep, and all fled from the prison to the most holy tomb of Saint Martial the bishop. And so by the prayers of the blessed man they were freed from prison and from death.

XII. Let what profited the eyes profit the ears of the people of God. The daughter of the aforesaid Nivardus, named Actefledis, had lost the light of her eyes, so that she could not see at all. One day she was brought by her parents to the man of God Aredius, and he was entreated that she might be given light. And when they prostrated themselves at the priest's feet, then the holy man, having signed her eyes and praying to the Lord within himself, she was at once restored to health, and she who had been led along by a guide returned to her homeland as a guide [herself].

XIII. The examples of the just also instruct their followers more eagerly than the preaching of many. Once when the man of God was hastening to Burgundy to the king for a charitable cause, he was earnestly invited by Duke Antestius to turn aside to his house, where his daughter lay half-dead in her little bed. As she was breathing out her last breath, the man of God Aredius entered the house, offered a prayer for her, and the girl, gladdening the house by obtaining a remedy, came back from her passing. For he who ordered the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue to be raised within her chamber granted the dead girl to the one who asked him, so that she returned from death to life. A certain woman named Bessa, her limbs crippled by infirmity, her fingers drawn in, her joints bent, feeble in her steps, prayed lying prostrate to be healed, devout, suppliant, wasted away. At once, touched by Aredius's holy hand with the cross, the length of her legs was stretched out, the sinews were loosened into their proper working, and her limbs, long awaited, at last deserved to know themselves again. And so by the prayers of the holy man she was made well.

Let praises be recorded which are justly reckoned to his palm. A certain woman, already thought near to death, bore a wound on her neck; she came to the holy man, begging him to arm it with the banner of the holy cross, for she feared to die. And when he pressed the sign of Christ upon the wound, suddenly the worms died, and the woman returned in health.

XIV. When we behold the greater miracles of the saints, we are turned the more earnestly to the love of God. For a girl from the city of Périgueux came to the man of God, so contracted that her legs, stuck to her heels, touched them, long since condemned [never] to walk; and the most holy man did not let her go before her sickness let her go, and she who had before gone on her hands walked on her feet. So he asked her carefully whether she had hope in Christ, whether she believed she would one day be healed. And when she affirmed her faith in all things, Aredius fixed his knees on the ground and prayed at length; then, stretching his eyes and his hands together towards heaven, he reminded the Lord Jesus Christ with the fullest faith of his promise, which says: Whatever you ask believing, it will be done for you (Mark 11:23[–24]); and: If you have faith, you will not only do these signs, but you will do greater than these (John 14:12). And when he had asked this with full strength and devotion, he turned to the girl and said: If you believe faithfully, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ rise and stand on your feet. And at once she rose, and her feet and limbs were made firm, and she was made well from that hour.

Likewise another woman came to him from the same city, condemned by a similar infirmity; and when she had been handled by the holy man's hand, she returned home upright, and as an older woman she ran the road which as a young woman she had not travelled.

XV. As often as we raise the mind to the heights of almighty God, the things we see on earth grow worthless to the mind, so that, having received grace from God, we may enter the heavenly homeland; as, for instance, this man, who is adorned with such great powers, is not darkened by earthly contagion.

A certain man called Addo, son of one Proculus, came into the presence of the most blessed man so crippled that he walked on his heels instead of his soles, and the parts so unhappily stuck together could not be separated; he then sought remedies from Saint Aredius. And he, having placed the sign of the cross upon him, the man who had come lame on his knees was straightened on his feet, and walking, was brought back to the soles of his feet.

XVI. Let there be added the powers of his works, by which they are believed to be true. A certain man from the territory of Bourges, with contracted sinews and crippled in his step, came hurrying to the monastery and begged for help, that the holy man might come to his aid. The man of God Aredius took up the cause for the sake of reward; when a prayer had been poured out for him with a blessing, what the holy hand had touched returned in health.

XVII. Let the page gain what grace bestows. A certain Leonacter was made so mad by an insanity of the body that it was believed to be nothing other than rabies; his very horrible fury could not be borne, even though he was bound hand and foot very tightly in chains, and, overpowered by force, was further constrained with fetters, and on top of this the pain of the punishment crushed him; and so, raging cruelly, he was at last brought to the saint of God Aredius. Without any delay, armed on the forehead with the sign of the cross, in a moment he was freed from the ancient enemy and from his chains together; afterwards he became a cleric, and rendered service to Christ with song in better works. But it is done by the wonderful dispensation of almighty God, that those whom divine rewards do not invite to better things are taught by temporal scourges.

XVIII. At the same time as the soldier of Christ was living on earth, Ferreolus, a venerable bishop, was present in the city of Limoges as shepherd to govern the people entrusted to him; and as often as this bishop was oppressed by fevers, or worn down in severe pain by some sickness, he would send messengers to the man of God Aredius, that he might intercede more fully for him with the Lord. Having celebrated vigils for him, he obtained [healing] for the shepherd, the venerable abbot for the bishop, the lowly and humble for the exalted. And because the growing page covers greater miracles, let the mystery concerning a certain blind man made bright be brought forward. A certain man, robbed of light and long oppressed by darkness, clouded with thick gloom, was led to the blessed man's cell, feeling his way with his foot; when the holy man saw him he took pity on him and restored his sight by praying, and he returned to his region now lit up with clear light.

XIX. It is pleasing to bring forward what was glorious to memory. A certain man named Witrimundus, called Atto, had been afflicted so cruelly with toothache that the pain pressing upon him gave him no respite at all. Then, coming to the holy man while he was devoutly making his visit to blessed Martin, he was asked why one of his jaws seemed more swollen, and he answered that he was tormented by a most severe toothache; then the man of God felt the swollen face with the gentlest touch, saying: You will be healed by the Lord, through the intercession of Martin, most faithful servant of God. And so, as soon as the speech begun by the just man was finished, health was poured back into the tooth, and the pain was cured together with the swelling.

XX. A certain woman, Ricovera by name, wife of a moneyer of Tours, had faithfully offered the holy man a half-full flask of oil to be blessed; then Aredius, having made the sign of the cross, and bringing out of the chrismarium another flask, in which was contained some of the oil of blessed Martin, poured a drop onto the half-full flask, and the power leapt up in such a flood of oil that, the flask being filled, she had to take the oil elsewhere, so that nothing of the overflowing blessing might be lost. This blessing profited both equally: him who gave to the one who asked, and her who asked what she deserved.

XXI. This too is granted to few, that a soldier of Christ should be loved for such great miracles. For the most reverend man had resolved, in order to win the palm of the heavenly homeland, to go to Tours for the feast of the blessed bishop. And so at one time it happened that the holy man was hastening to the aforesaid city. Now while the bishop of that city with his clergy was earnestly performing the office of psalmody in the church at night, his deacon, while singing in the church, was overcome by sleep; and when the bishop saw him sleeping, he said to him: Why are you sleeping, brother? Waking from sleep, he said: I saw you, my lord, going out of the church and hastening to meet the blessed man Aredius. And the deacon had scarcely finished speaking when at once a wicked spirit in a certain man cried out that it could not bear the presence of Saint Aredius. Hearing this, the bishop knew that the man of the Lord Aredius was arriving; and at once the bishop went out to meet the abbot before the doors of the church with lighted candles, and with great joy and exultation they entered the church, and continued in the divine offices almost the whole night. For many sick people, or those bound by various infirmities, returned home in sound strength through his prayers and intercessions. At another time again, when he had come to Tours for the same feast, and the man of God Aredius was handling the legs of a certain paralytic with gentle application, he testified that he had seen the hand of Saint Martin, how it straightened the crippled limbs, and so, as the saint's right hand touched him, the paralytic at once stood straight on his own feet. Such a power of cures, conferred on him by divine grace, shone out that whatever sick person came went away healed and sound in full strength. And to the possessed health was restored so swiftly that, from so huge a multitude, not all their names could be written down.

XXII. If his miracles are reviewed one by one, it is not at all unfitting that the words of so great a power should be believed. At one time the man of God, having come out of the basilica when the night vigils were finished, saw a globe of light come down from heaven onto his own cell; and believing that this brightness was made by a man, the man of God asked his disciple who it was that was walking through the garden with a torch at such an hour. Meanwhile, as he was wondering, the very globe that had appeared above the cell at once rolled back to the stars, and he, with fear and trembling, his hands spread out, gave thanks to the divine power for the light. Then he was asked by the monk who was seeing this with him what this miracle was, a vision of such brightness, that the mysteries of the most blessed priest should be revealed in such a way. The holy man answered him: Be silent, be silent, foolish one; know that most blessed Martin visits this cell by his special favour, and returns to the heavens with the glory of shining light. Now it was fitting that he whom divine grace protected should receive a visitation through the illumination of the Holy Spirit; but the friend of God, guarding against the vice of boasting, ordered his disciple to tell this vision to no one until he had passed to the Lord. Thus the faithful soldier kept the rule of his master, the Mediator of God, who, transfigured on the mountain, ordered the disciples to tell no one the vision which they had seen until the Son of Man had risen from the dead. Consider, then, with how great a fire of love for God and neighbour this man was kindled, who by the revelation of the Spirit was divinely found worthy to receive such a gift. For God is a consuming fire (Deut. 4:24; Heb. 12:29), as James testifies, who says: Every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights (James 1:17).

XXIII. These things having been done thus, the holy man remained continually intent on the divine offices. For the enemy of the human race could find nothing in him to deceive by fraud, nor anything to darken by pretence. He was indeed generous in almsgiving, devout in prayer, diligent in vigils, abundant in humility, outstanding in teaching, peaceable in discourse, cautious in speech, most holy in his way of life, strong in harsh sufferings, cheerful in good works, most secure in temptation, most open-handed in hospitality, beneficent amid hatreds, and in prosperity and adversity alike ever intent on heaven, perfect in charity, which is the bond of the perfection of Christ (Col. 3:14). The sincerity of his mind he showed by the serenity of his face, and the gentleness of his heart he displayed in the mildness of his speech. Nothing was graver than his laughter, nothing at all sweeter than his sadness, nothing more merciful than his spirit, nothing kinder towards the humble. If he saw a poor man, he supported him; if a rich man, he urged him to do good, calling God to witness that he did all these things for His name, continually remembering what the Truth says in the Gospel: Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy (Matt. 5:7); and also this: Nevertheless give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you (Luke 11:41); and elsewhere: As water quenches fire, so alms quench sin (Ecclus. 3:33). Continually remembering these precepts, he fulfilled them most earnestly, and he was the foot of the lame and the eye of the blind, the father of orphans, the comforter of widows. What blind man did he not call his heir, or what cripple did his hand not support? He went about continually accompanied by this army; in them too, seeing Christ, he longed to embrace himself; and giving them clothing, he believed he was covering the limbs of Christ under the garment of the needy; and for this reason, sharing his money with his Lord, he rejoiced to make his substance a partnership with Christ, so that Christ might make him co-heir of the heavenly kingdoms, knowing indeed that it is written that that is the good inheritance which is kept with the Lord as guardian. For his counsels among his own people were nothing other than divine teachings and the foundations of the sacred Scriptures. For it is fitting that the good should love and imitate, and the guilty fear, him whom divine power illumined, so that the gift received from God, with honey-sweet teaching, seasoned by the Holy Spirit, salted with longing for Christ, and ever concerned for eternal blessedness.

XXIV. If we consider what and how great things almighty God worked through his priest, a page of the pen is set out at greater length. The wicked, flattering with evil counsels, are often wont to subvert the hearts of earthly kings, according to the word of Solomon: Evil conversations corrupt good morals (1 Cor. 15:33). At one time it happened that tributes or a census had been assessed upon the peoples by the kings. This condition was imposed with the utmost rigour on all the cities established throughout the Gauls. On this account the most reverend man, moved by compassion, hastened to the king's presence, to make representation for the citizens who had been entered by public edict for a heavy census. But since it is written: The heart of the king is in the hand of the Lord (Prov. 21:1), whatever the holy man asked, he obtained from the devoted king. It happened, then, that as he was returning from his journey, coming to a certain village, Catuliacum, on the very day on which the holy mysteries of the Lord's resurrection were being celebrated, he was invited by the people and began to devote himself to the holy offices. While he was celebrating the divine solemnities, a certain girl, who was grievously oppressed by demons, cried out that she could not endure the presence of the holy man, and yet, though he was unknown to her, she called on his name. He, practising works of compassion according to his usual custom, when the divine mysteries were finished, fled to the harbour of prayer, and stood by as intercessor so that the girl might no longer be tormented by the ancient enemy. For there were in her seven most wicked spirits; and as he devoted himself to prayer, he at once drove out five demons by his entreaty. As two still remained, the most blessed man ordered the girl's parents that she should not leave the church until what remained of the malignant adversary should be expelled from her body. So the holy man, coming to the church where he had ordered her to stay, taking his monks with him, lay prostrate in prayer and was able to obtain from the Lord that the two demons which had remained were driven out, so that with a sound mind and settled senses she returned home.

XXV. At another time also, when the man of God, on account of a condition of the same kind, sought the king's presence by an almost secret arrival, he hastened on his journey. And when he had entered the walls of the city of Paris, the people of this city were suffering from a heavy fever, dysentery, and a most grievous disease, so that the number of bodies, because of the multitude dying each day, especially the crowd of infants, could not be reckoned. One day, while he was being venerated, not undeservedly, with affection by the bishop of that city, [the bishop] asked him to stay with him a few days out of charity, so that he might be an intercessor for the people before the Lord. So, when the man of God Aredius was willing to comply with his requests, it happened that some of his own men fell gravely ill with the same most grievous sickness. The most blessed man, secure in the Lord in steadfast confidence, prayed with his usual prayer for the people of that city, and did not cease to console them with gentle exhortation in his sermons, so that no one should despair of the mercy of the Lord's compassion. He ordered blessed oil to be brought to him, and with his own hand, with the sign of the cross, he anointed the mouths and nostrils of each, saying to them: Take comfort in the Lord, and encourage one another, brothers; the right hand of Christ restores you all to health; and he spoke thus to his own men, saying: Do not, I beg you, my brothers, do not be saddened, but rather strengthen yourselves manfully, and trust more earnestly in the mercy of the Lord, for the divine power restores you all in health to your own region; meanwhile he was turning over in his mind where he might learn the king to be, so that, having inquired, he might seek him out. So, leaving the brothers in that city, he hastened with a few companions, making his way as far as [a place] called Brinnacum. While, without doubt, he was standing there as a traveller, he said to those following him: Know that the king is hard pressed by a heavy fever, and the end of his life is now almost upon him, but the mercy of the Lord, out of regard for the poor, will free him when we visit him for his healing. Keep this also secret. But after these few days his children, who still seem to be well, will depart from this world. By the spirit of prophecy the man of God Aredius knew what the outcome afterwards proved. When the holy servant of God reached the place mentioned, the king, learning of his arrival, ordered him to be brought into his bedchamber, believing that he would be helped in the Lord by his prayers. Accordingly, when he had entered and the duty of greeting had been rendered, he began to feel him with his hands, while within himself he was asking the Lord in prayer that the king might give assent to his petitions. When [the king] began to feel easier from the distress of his illness under the holy hands of the most blessed man, [Aredius] set out the cause of his business; and with the favour of God, who rules all things and orders all things sweetly, whatever the priest of God asked of the king he was able to win by easy grant. And the king, adding further, handed over into his hands the very books in which the people of his kingdom, entered for a heavy census, were held oppressed, out of regard for the holy man and for his own security, so that he might burn them in the fire on his own authority. Then Aredius, having received the books, ordered coals to be prepared. When this was done, taking the books in his own hands, he burned them in the fire, with many standing around. Having obtained the object of his petition, then, after the third day he bade the prince farewell.

XXVI. One day, before he reached Paris, the outcome there confirmed what he had told his companions not long before. When a messenger reported it, the man of God learned for certain that the king's sons, whose deaths he had foretold earlier, had died, and were to be carried to Paris with a great funeral throng. When, on his way back, he had come some distance toward that city, he found the people of that city already freed from the disease of dysentery by divine help. He also found one of his companions, named Constantine, lying in grave danger of death. Some, whom he found had died, he restored to health by his prayers. Then he was urged by his people to entrust the man who had succumbed to that dreadful sickness to someone in some place, so that when he passed from this light he might be enclosed in a mound of turf in the earth, so near was he already to approaching death. But the most blessed man, moved by compassion and ready with his usual kindness, lifted him onto the carriage in which he himself used to sit, and [Constantine] was driven under another's guidance. When he was already on the third day of the journey, overcome by the sickness and struck by the blow of death, he fell lifeless to the ground. When the most blessed man saw this, pierced to the heart, he began to give himself to prayer more earnestly, with groans and tears. When he rose from prayer, he turned to the body, and as he felt him with his hands, [the man] began to open his eyes; and not long hours afterward, the prey of death having been won back, he was restored unharmed to his former light; he who had been despaired of was restored to lasting health. Then in a faint voice he asked for water to be given him. While all wandered here and there, anxiously searching, they found none at all, because that place was certainly without water; but the holy priest of God, turning aside a little and striking the ground with a blow of his staff, made water spring up abundantly. He at once brought it in a small vessel to the man asking for it. So the burning of thirst was quenched, the pallor was driven from his face, his countenance turned ruddy, he rose to his feet; and he who had been condemned to the fall of death was presented safe to his homeland. Afterwards he lived out the course of many years.

XXVII. To the miracles of his powers must be added [one] by whose example the hearts of the hearers may be enlightened. When he was already drawing near to his homeland at a certain village, Argentomagus, a certain Artemius, one of the monks, suggested at a fitting moment that food ought to be prepared for the brothers. He said to him: 'Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added to you' (Luke 12:31); and that saying of the Psalmist: 'But those who seek the Lord shall not lack any good thing' (Ps. 33:10). 'But take this from me, dearest brother: when you have crossed the bed of this river, lift your eyes to the right-hand side, and you will find a convenient place where we can relieve the want of hunger for ourselves and our beasts.' And when he came to the place he had been directed to, he found there two fish of wonderful size, still very much alive. When they had been roasted, Aredius, the man of God, took a portion of them for refreshment, and most of them were seen to eat of them to their fill. But he in whose name the apostles let down their nets in the waves, and were not able to draw them in for the multitude of fish, distributed food to these hungry men as well.

XXVIII. When the powers of the saints are recounted again, the minds of the faithful, as if thirsting, long to be filled with the depths of God's mysteries. Once, while he was on a journey making his way, approaching a certain village, Argentomagus, he addressed those following him, saying: 'Let us pass by quietly, so that no delay is caused to our journey.' For this was a profane place, consecrated by ancient superstition to the cults of demons, and in that place the Christian people living there could not bear their misery, because they were subject to various infirmities, or were even continually harassed by the demons themselves. And when Aredius, the man of God, wished to slip away from the people unnoticed, and was praying in secret, the multitude of the sick people was stirred and called upon his very name, because the insolent crowd of demons could not hide itself from the coming of the holy man. So, as the multitude of the ailing people followed him, he looked back behind him, stood still, and at once prostrated himself on the ground in earnest prayer, asking the Lord for them that they might be saved according to their faith. And when he had risen from prayer and had straightaway made the sign of the cross over each one, then those who were held by various ailments, and those who were harassed by unclean spirits, as he applied oil with a blessing, gave thanks to the Lord and were freed from their infirmities or from the demons to their former health.

XXIX. Those whom God chose before the foundation of the world, the loftiness of the reprobate despises. This holy man was cast down among men and the least in the sight of the world, but was raised up as the greatest among the hosts of the saints. Once, when he was on a journey, as one day was declining toward evening, not far from a village called Moenum, he ordered that the journey be halted and that the packs the beasts were carrying be unloaded in a suitable place; and when they had seen a pleasant place, a space delightful to look at for staying in, the most blessed man, knowing by the spirit of prophecy what was later to come upon them, exhorted with fatherly address his companions, over whom he knew very great harm was hanging, and spoke to them, saying: 'Men, brothers and sons, believe that we shall suffer much harm this night; but take courage, and trust that we shall be delivered by heavenly help.' And without any delay, while the sky was seen to be most clear with starry brightness, suddenly the earth was shaken with thunder, and as if from its firmness was turned to trembling by the heavy noise; then the clouds were stirred up in the air and appeared in a dark colour across the stars; and those that had been shining with brightness were turned into driving rain; lightning flashed again and again from the sky, which had been darkened. Now not far from them were three idols dedicated to pagan worship; when the air was assailed by the lightning, in the onset of the thunder they were so overthrown from heaven that on the following day no foundations of the idols could be found. With the same stroke of lightning, as the fire flashed, a huge fire partly burned up a forest that could be seen by them in the distance, and the force of the winds tore up the trees and laid them flat. But those who were with the man of God were so terrified with fear that no one believed he could escape, fearing that the stroke of God would come down upon them. So he repeatedly urged his people to persist in prayer and to continue all night in the office of psalm-singing. Now the spot where Aredius, the man of God, had turned aside to stay seemed lower than the others where the rest had pitched their tents. All were so drenched by the vast quantity of water that nothing was left in their clothing through which the rush of water had not run; but the holy priest of God, looking round at his companions, placed the little case with the holy relics which he carried hung from his neck on top of the cloak and bedding where he was to rest, and that spot was as if touched by the heat of the sun, so that it felt no wetness at all.

XXX. Nor should that be passed over in silence which befits his power. It happened once, when war had arisen between two princes, that [men] set out to break the walls of the city of Limoges, the people of that region being afraid, and to reduce it to desolation and destroy it; messengers had been sent to them by the king to whose rule the people were to be subjected, and the city, already laid waste, was under siege. So one of them, named Domaricus, who had come with others to seize the city, approached the holy man of God, questioning him with careful concern, that he should foretell whatever future things he had come to know by the spirit of revelation. To them he spoke thus in private: 'Although I know that you fear King Theodebert, know this: that his kingdom will shortly be taken away, and indeed he will very soon be killed. But your king will stir up the forces of many nations against him, and over him the victory will be given him; yet, having won the battle and the victory, he will be treacherously deceived, but his kingdom will be handed over to his sons and grandsons to govern. The other kings, whose kingdom seems to stand firm, will be overtaken by the moment of death and snatched from the world in dishonour.' And the aforesaid Domaricus went back to the warriors. And what Aredius, the man of God, foretold, the outcome of events afterwards proved true. Besides these other good things, speech of wisdom and knowledge had been abundantly granted him; he possessed charity and humility above all; and he did not oppress his servants as slaves, but loved them with kindly charity. Why should I dwell on more? In all his way of life he shone like the morning star gleaming among the stars of heaven, like a great lamp. For he always emulated the perfect in good, and always set before himself the virtues of others as an example. He was slow to speak and swift to hear, and he was rich in alms, very long-suffering in charity, lofty in humility, subtle in speech, watchful in mind, ready in eloquence, burning with zeal, truly a useful vessel in the house of Christ.

XXXI. It is fitting to believe of many of the saints that, prophesying things to come through the Spirit of prophecy by clear insight, they are told of as having done things by divine power. So too this man of God, enlightened by heavenly grace, announced through the revelation of the Holy Spirit what was to come upon men. A certain man among the citizens of the city of Limoges, surnamed Nectarius, not poor in goods but rich in wealth, had an only son, and the blessed servant of God perceived that the onset of death was suddenly threatening him. Therefore the most reverend man sent a messenger to his parents, that before the boy succumbed to death he should be brought into his presence. Then the mother, on hearing the message, burst into tears for the destruction of her offspring. Meanwhile, with a few servants attending her, she obeyed the blessed man's command; and as she was making her way, so that the truth of the one who foretold it might be proved, the boy's limbs, seized by a great force of fever, went slack, and with head drooping and eyes closed he seemed almost dead. And while the holy man was awaiting the outcome of this matter, the servants, seeing the youth lifeless, at once burst into weeping and cried out, and came hurrying with the greatest haste to the man of God. Moved by compassion, he took up the lifeless boy and decided to lay him before the sacred relics of the blessed bishop Hilary. He commended him to the Lord with great prayers and entreaties, that he who restored Lazarus, four days dead, alive from the tomb, might graciously come to the aid of this boy too. When the prayer was finished, he who had been seen to be lifeless was at once restored unharmed to his mother; and she who had believed she would hand him over dead to burial returned home with him, joyful and rejoicing with great gladness.

XXXII. These things, then, and very many others like them, which it would take too long to go through one by one, Aredius, the man of the Lord, adorned with the grace of prophecy, frequently foretold. For there are many works of power that almighty God made manifest through this most blessed man; and the more often they are turned over, the more those things grow which may be beheld in the miracles. But these, namely those [told] above, are a few gathered from many. Living on earth as a sojourner, after he won the heavenly palm and, drawn out of the snare of the world, returned to Christ, he left us an example no less worth relating than what he could have done while living in the world. But it would now take long to recount in words the miracles of his powers one by one, especially since the book, already filled beyond measure and calling for an end, rejects [further] speech, and the dryness of our speech, worn thin and almost exhausted by the long road, gives way: not that we have set out everything that was to be told of him, for no one can reach even a hundredth part of the works of his powers, of how great the adornments of good works, which are very great and precious, that [God] by the privilege of heavenly reward conferred on the blessed man. This, then, remains, that we may be able to reach the end of our course. O man truly to be imitated! O how his example is to be preferred to all! O blessed seed after Abraham! Abraham's blessing indeed earned a son, but Aredius, being blessed, is carried over into the heavenly kingdom; Abraham handed on an heir, this man no less an inheritance; lastly, Abraham offered up the pledge he had, but Aredius committed everything he could have in the world to the will and authority of the Lord. Let it suffice, then, to have said this. Now, as I hope, we have drawn out a lengthy discourse, though with a rustic understanding, although we could by no means suffice to tell the praises worthy of his merits. But now I think it worthy, for the edification of hearers as well as of readers, if I take care to set out in a few words how he passed from this life to the Lord, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns in the unity of the Holy Spirit for ever and ever, amen.
HERE BEGINS [THE ACCOUNT] OF THE PASSING OF THE HOLY AND MOST BLESSED ABBOT AND CONFESSOR AREDIUS.

XXXIII. So when the man of the Lord had now reached old age, when he had already borne the adversities of the world and all its labours with an even mind, after he had heaped up on every side the merits of the most faithful stewardship entrusted to him, after manifold works of mercy, after the subjection of monks and monasteries [to his rule], after the sweet examples of his life, after the miracles of all good things and powers made manifest: his age now declining, when he was more than eighty years old, knowing that the dissolution of his body was now at hand, he said to his monks: 'Know, dearest brothers, that the Lord will soon deign to free me from the snare of this world.' When they heard this, all of them, melting at these words and turned to anguish, began to say mournfully: 'May it not befall your servants to see this, lord; rather may Christ allow Your Beatitude to flourish here for many years for the adornment of the Church.' But he, with tears and long sighs, said to them: 'Not our will, but rather the Lord's be done in this.' Then, as all mourned at these words, he said: 'Do not, I beg you, my brothers, do not be saddened, but rather rejoice and exult, for I have long desired this time; I have longed to receive this release.' So, as they were turned to anguish and sighing, and also held in uncertainty about the matter, the conversation ceased. Then, without any delay, after this a very slight fever spread through his body and he began to weary. Then, calling a certain servant, he gave him orders, saying: 'Hurry, my son, go quickly to the illustrious man Astidius, and tell him to come at a swift pace, because he himself will receive the charge of governing this monastery after the day of my death.' And again he said: 'For if he makes any delay, he will no longer see my face in this life.' The messenger indeed carried out the orders, but the aforesaid Astidius was slow to come. When he arrived, he no longer found the man of God surviving in this world. And so, as the man of God foretold, the outcome of events afterwards proved true. Meanwhile, as I had begun to say, when the blessed man was lying in his last illness, he did not cease even then from the work of God, reckoning this a good consummation of his virtues, if he carried it through to the end. For, spending whole nights in prayers and vigils, with his limbs failing, he compelled his spirit and mind to serve God, and, exceedingly glad, he awaited the longed-for journey. So when he felt the day was now near, he gathered his disciples on the ninth day before the Kalends of September, whom he was now beginning to leave in body, not in spirit, and said to them: 'Would that, dearest brothers, [you would be willing] to hear the counsel of my littleness. If you truly love me, love the warnings of Christ; fear continually the dreadful judgements of God. Take heed, with anxious consideration, of what kind you will be when presented on the day of judgement. For I am now going my way; and I too desire to be dissolved and, if the Lord permits, to be at rest.' When he had said this, as all were weeping and wailing, he said to them: 'See, today I commend into your hands the salvation of your souls: remember, then, my admonition, and all of you take thought for yourselves. Do constantly these things that I say, go over them often, and always keep the memory of me with you. Aredius will no longer be with you in this world.' When all who stood around heard this, raising great groans and weeping, they all wept with one voice, saying: 'Why are you deserting us, father, or why do you want to leave us so soon? We know indeed that you long for Christ, but your rewards are safe for you; have pity on us too, whom you are deserting. We cannot bear your absence, for we shall never afterwards have anyone like you. Let it grieve you, father, not to leave us orphans so soon.' As they lamented thus, that most loving shepherd watered his face abundantly with tears; and since he was loving, he could neither desert these men nor be separated any longer from Christ. At last, then, taking up his words again amid bitter tears, he said: 'Do not be saddened by this, and do not, I beg, be troubled any more with weeping over my departure; you ought rather to rejoice than to mourn, for though I shall be absent in body, I shall be present in spirit. I, for my part, if I could do anything, have laboured for your progress; and although I am weak, yet the Lord is for ever. To him I commend you, and to him I entrust the care of you. I know indeed that, as a useless servant, I have not done what I ought, but the Lord knows how I wished [to do it].' After these words too, as the day was now declining, he suddenly fell to the floor and, with his eyes raised to heaven, he prayed humbly, groaning and sighing: 'I commend to you, Lord Jesus, the sheep that you entrusted to me.' So, commending to the Lord with interest the gift of the talent he had received from him, and now placed at his last, he called his disciples to him, embraced them one by one, [kissing them?], and bidding all farewell, said: 'I shall no longer speak to you; you will see my face no more; and so fare well in peace, and know that I am at rest.' Those who stood around, hearing this, could in no way restrain themselves from weeping. Yet amid bitter tears these words alone scarcely sounded: 'We grieve indeed for our own sake, that by your departure you leave us without comfort; but for your sake, best of fathers, we are consoled, because after the labour of this world you are going to eternal rest.' Then, with his eyes raised to heaven, he poured out a silent prayer, and then said with tears: 'Remember me, Lord, who alone are without sin, Redeemer of the world, and bring me out of the body of death, and save me into your heavenly kingdom: you are my protector, Lord; into your hands I commend my spirit. Receive me, then, according to your great mercy, and do not confound me in my expectation; but help me, and aid the departure of my soul. Open to me, Lord, as I hasten, the gate of your kingdom, and let the princes of darkness not meet me, but let your clemency protect and defend [me], and let your hand lead me to a place of refreshment and consolation, even if into the last tabernacle which you have prepared for those who fear your holy name.' Amid this he also added, saying: 'Now, Lord, let your servant depart in peace, according to your word.' And when he had said this, he gave up his spirit amid the words of prayer (Luke 2:29).

XXXIV. When that holy soul had cast off the burden of the flesh, at once, since it was the second hour of the night, a globe shining with exceeding brightness was seen to have come down from heaven over his cell, and then to pass up from there to the stars. In this way, then, his holy soul, freed from earthly contagion, flew back joyfully to its Maker, led by the holy angels. The man had given up his spirit, and the mourning made for him resounded to heaven. The body was laid out according to custom and placed on a bier, and there they passed the whole night watching in psalms and hymns. When the light of day had risen, a multitude of people gathered; and when it had also come to the knowledge of the bishop of the city of Limoges, on hearing it he came hurrying with great weeping and at a swift pace, and wept for a very long time over the body of the holy man, because he had not found him alive in the world; and presently, when he wished to carry [it] to the church of the holy martyr Julian, which the holy man had built, where the sacred body lay, they could in no way lift the bier even a little. For Aredius, the man of the Lord, had determined to give his body to burial in the church of the holy bishop Hilary, which he too had built by his own work. Then Bishop Ferreolus, made very sad, proclaimed a three-day fast to be kept with psalm-singing. When this was done, he himself with his people kept the fast without ceasing through those three days. Then, when the fast was completed, he said: 'If it is the will of the Lord or of this saint that he go where I and this people wish, let him be lifted without any delay.' Now the place was in a more secluded part. And when they had come to the bier to try to lift him, it was at once lifted with such ease that it was easily carried by two, which before could not be moved even by many. All who were present with the bishop, seeing this, magnified the glory of Christ with great exultation, saying: 'Great and wonderful are your works, Lord God almighty.' And when the body had now been carried to the tomb, all who were present could in no way restrain themselves from weeping; they cried out that they were losing a father, and amid tears and sobs could scarcely bring out these words: 'Why are you deserting us, father, and to whom are you handing over your foster-children to be ruled?' So, the body having been given to burial according to custom, the aforesaid bishop returned home. Let there be compared, then, if you please, with the obsequies of this holy man, which I will call not a funeral but rather a triumph, the empty glory of the world; let the pomp of rich men, too, be set beside it, if it can be equalled with this dead priest. Those men the madness of crowds honours with confused applause; Aredius, stripped of the world's distress, angels bear with heavenly praises to the everlasting kingdoms. Those men after the world's pomps are thrust into Tartarus; this man after the world's adversities is joyfully received in Abraham's bosom. Those men, weighed down by the wealth of riches, are cast down at death into Gehenna; but Aredius, exalted by his alms, will rise in glory with the saints. Those men at the last lament, condemned in hell; Aredius, crowned with the laurel, exults in the Church with all the saints since the world began. Thanks be to you, our God, who have repaid him great things for small, and have made him rest in everlasting glory, and in that promise of the Gospel, where it says: 'Well done, good and faithful servant, because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many' (Matt. 25:21), he has here deserved to hear: 'Enter into the joy of your Lord.' And as it is written of such men through Solomon: 'The just man is delivered out of distress' (Prov. 11:8). And it is written through Jeremiah: 'Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord will be his confidence' (Jer. 17:7). Hence David too says: 'His will is in the law of the Lord, and he will be like a tree that is planted beside the running waters' (Ps. 1:2–3). Hence also the Lord says through the prophet Isaiah: 'I have called him and blessed him, and his way is made straight' (Isa. 48:15). Hence too it is said in the book of Ecclesiasticus: 'It will go well at the last with him who fears the Lord; on the day of his death he will be blessed' (Ecclus. 1:13). Hence also it is written elsewhere: 'Glorious will be the fruit of his good labours' (Wisd. 3:15), and 'his crown triumphs for ever' (Wisd. 4:2). Let it suffice for us to have told this of the death of the holy man, so that I may not weary the readers. And as his life is ended, so let our discourse also be ended.
HERE BEGIN [THE ACCOUNTS] OF THE MIRACLES OF THE HOLY ABBOT AREDIUS.

35. Now, of the many miracles which the Lord constantly works by his merits at his most holy body, I shall undertake, for the readers' convenience, at least a few out of the many which Jesus Christ made manifest there at the close of his death; and indeed the human mind is not able to burst out in words [to tell] with how great mysteries heavenly grace makes its soldiers illustrious. One of the monks from the most holy man's cell, named Baudenus, did not delay to go to the region of Burgundy with the charters by which the monastery's possessions were confirmed. There, then, seeking out the venerable and distinguished prelate Syagrius, bishop of the city of Autun, he implored him with his prayers, since he was held most worthy of honour above all in the king's palace, that by his patronage the cell might be protected from the plots of various rivals. He, assenting to the requests of the aforesaid monk, the most reverend man did not refuse what he asked: but also, by royal authority, he granted [him] the instruments and the freedom to return to [his] region. And when very many days had passed, and he was hurrying back with his request obtained, he entered a town of the region of Limoges. One day, in a certain village named Ricomagus, he found there the magnificent man Nectarius; and he disclosed to him all that the outcome had granted to his petitions. While meanwhile he was being questioned by him, he began to falter in his speech, and with his mind gone and a raging face, breaking out at once into speech, he could not keep silent the cause of his deed, that he had been shamefully defiled by the vice of adultery. While he gnashed his teeth and tore himself with his bites, he shook off from himself in agitation the chrismarium which the most blessed man Aredius had been accustomed to carry, and which held relics of the saints, and threw it on the ground. And since his great frenzy could in no way be calmed, he was bound and handed over to guards. Meanwhile one of the servants of the aforesaid man, picking up the chrismarium which he had thrown from himself, unknowingly put it away among the clothes. While this was being done, with the baggage packed together, they began to load a pack animal. But when the load had been lifted onto it, pressed down by the sacred weight, it fell to the ground and could not move a step further. What more? It was put on another, which, having taken up the weight, in the same way likewise fell down on the ground. And though it was driven on bloodied by many goads, it in no way recovered the spirit to rise, until occasion was given for the fault of the misdeed, once understood, to be revealed. Then, while he was driven more fiercely by the onset of his frenzy, he cried out that the chrismarium, which he said he had carried unworthily, was bound up with his clothes; and therefore the beast would not move unless it were taken away from there, where rather the fault of negligence lay. This they found at once on searching the bag, and out of reverent devotion and piety the exalted man Nectarius placed it with honour and reverence on an innocent boy; at once the [delayed] hours of the journey were released. For the aforesaid Baudenus, since before he was disturbed in spirit, as indeed can be judged of no other than one who was not governed by his own senses, took to flight in front of everyone with long strides. And when in the space of one hour he had run swiftly on his own feet almost twelve miles, his body exhausted, he fell half-dead to the ground: and when he had been overtaken by the guards, he was put in a lodging. When the night had passed, rising at dawn, he presented himself, compelled by the unclean spirit, at the most holy tomb of Saint Martial; and there, as he disclosed the confession of his deed, the evil spirit was driven out, and he was found worthy to receive the remedy of health.

36. There are also many other things which almighty God has worked after the passing of the holy man. On such an occasion, while the people were waiting, one of the household came in great haste to the aforesaid magnificent man and announced that his wife was held in grave danger of death, and urged him to come quickly, if he wished to find her alive. He, meanwhile, trusting in the Lord's mercy, ordered in haste the servant who had carried the holy man's chrismarium with him to hurry ahead. And when he had entered the house, the whole household was given over to grief and lamentation, because she lay at the point of so sudden a death. With her eyes closed, she showed the sign of one about to die by [the swelling of] her throat, where a very grievous lump had arisen. Her power of speech already shut off and her eyes dimmed, she could not even recognise her husband. But when the holy man's chrismarium was hung on the dying woman's neck, death was at once put to flight; immediately her eyes were opened to the light, the breath of her spirit was restored to its former health. Belching forcefully, the lump in her throat removed, she vomited up what she had not taken as food, and she who had had death at the door was restored to life. The chrismarium itself, with priests summoned, was carried with veneration to the holy man's monastery.

37. But who could tell in words, one by one, all the wonders which the Lord Jesus Christ constantly works at his holy tomb? One day a woman had resolved that she must go and see the holy man's presence, to give thanks. While the monks were celebrating the night vigils, a certain Babolenus, who had a son named Babolenus who had been afflicted with a grave injury of the limbs, [the boy] was carried by his parents and laid at the holy man's tomb; and as he lay on the pavement, about midnight the boy broke out into speech and felt the joints of his limbs joined again in the places where they had been loosened; and raising himself from the pavement, with his limbs made firm, he stood on his feet: and he who had been brought to the tomb in [others'] hands, rejoicing with his parent, went back home on his own feet, giving thanks to Christ.

38. It must be closely considered how great gifts of his grace almighty God has conferred on his saints in this life, so that, for a greater heap of glory, they may be rewarded in the heavenly homeland after the triumph. So a certain monk named Gaudomeres, of the monastery of Ambiacinum, which is situated not far from the city, was held by an evil spirit, so that he wanted to tear with his teeth any man he saw, and bound in two chains he was led in fetters like a criminal to a judge. One day he was brought to the holy man's tomb, and there, restored to his former health, he was snatched from the enemy adversary by whom he was tormented, [and] he turned many to the service of almighty God. For the chains with which the wretch was bound were loosed of their own accord, so that by a double miracle [God] might show that in one moment the tight chains were broken, and divine grace freed the man possessed by a demon, so that he might serve freely God, for whom every creature groans.
