Indeed, if anyone, as a case requires, has been bound or fettered with chains for any offence, if it happens that he is led bound along the public road that is near his basilica, as soon as they have come opposite that church, at once all his bonds burst and the accused is freed, and it does not permit him to be held bound any longer.

39. To wonderful things succeed things still more wonderful. One day two mutes came to the holy man's tomb, though they could not ask with the tongue, but [only] by faith. Anointed then with the oil, at the Lord's command the tongue of the mutes was at once loosed, and they began to speak, adoring, and those who had been made tongueless at once conversed with the people. The elect receive this indeed as a gift, that the more they abound in miracles, the more they judge themselves unworthy, lest they be carried away to vain glory and so be deprived of the heavenly gift. Then four men coming from various provinces, condemned to the same blindness, lay prostrate in the oratory awaiting light, seeking by this means the holy man's remedy. Meanwhile, as they offered prayers at the sacred tomb, asking with one accord, he at once opened the eyes of the blind, which had long been closed, and having obtained clear light, they made for the threshold of the church.

40. Many other signs and miracles are indeed worked there by his merits at the bidding of heavenly grace: among which also a lamp, overflowing, pours out oil abundantly. With this holy liquid many anointed there are healed of various infirmities, and the name of the Lord, the eternal God, is continually blessed there. And likewise at his bed, which is placed on his monastery's estate, many miracles are similarly shown. And also in various places, wherever his sacred relics are carried or to which they have been brought, very many signs of miracles are wrought abundantly, as the glory of Christ reveals his merits. We have thought it burdensome to pursue all these in order in words, and so we have embraced them in these very few syllables, since we are now hastening to cease from speaking. For if we now took care to unfold them one by one, as they were done, we would both exceed the measure of a very small volume and perhaps, by that very length, bring weariness on the readers. But what we have told too little of gives proof openly to all, as they see those many kinds of shackles of the fettered, which are seen hung at his tomb as evidence of the facts. Of these we have recorded either indeed few or almost none, simply because, being placed in the sight of all, just as we [know] the place, so all, we doubt not, know them. These indeed, very many, are established to have been done within a short time. As for those which are to be done hereafter through long spans of time, of what kind or how great they will be, who can now grasp by estimation, since even today miracles never cease to be done at the prelate's tomb? But daily the sick come to the holy man's tomb, and keeping vigil there are made well; the blind come and receive sight; the possessed come and are freed; perjurers come and either die or are tormented by the devil; those bound in iron take refuge and are released; the lame, brought in carts, their steps made firm, return home unharmed. Many cures indeed are accomplished by the liquid of the oil that increases there. How many, again, held by fevers or various infirmities, who had been captives of the enemy, have been freed after the passing of the most blessed man! But they cannot be added one by one to the page of this little book, lest it cause weariness to those weaker in faith, and too long a discourse be set forth for the doubters. Let it suffice, then, to have told these few out of many, so that the hearts of many believers, filled as if with various flowers fragrant in the bosom of holy Church, may be able to gather perfect fruits which worldly delight does not defile. For one cannot both rejoice here with the world and reign there with Christ, nor serve two masters, namely God and mammon. Putting off, then, the works of darkness, let us put on the armour of light, for the Creator of all is the true light, which enlightens every man coming into this world, through our Lord Jesus Christ his Son, who in perfect Trinity lives and reigns as God in the unity of the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

The Testament of St Aredius, although it is not found in the manuscript codex of St Gall, it nevertheless seemed best to give here rather than in the appendix, as we promised in the notes to chapter 29 of book 10 of the History, where he is praised by Gregory. It is now given complete for the first time, from the archive of St Martin of Tours.
THE TESTAMENT OF ST AREDIUS, ABBOT OF ATTANUM.

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, on the day before the Kalends of November, in the eleventh year of the reign of our lord King Sigibert, I, Aredius the priest, and Pelagia, of sound mind and sound judgement, sitting as judges and arbiters of our own property, fearing the chances of human frailty, lest the sudden occasion of death should forestall us, have made our testament, which I, Aredius myself, wrote with my own hand, and handed to a competent number of witnesses to be signed. And this our testament, if by chance it cannot be valid under civil or praetorian law, or by the provisions of any law, new or old, is ordered to be valid in the place of codicils and of all writings that stand firm. So that this may be done, given and performed, let it be kept unimpaired in all respects, according to the terms written below, which we have drawn up with the help of Christ the Lord.

Therefore we appoint you, holy Martin of Tours, as [our heir], so that [it be administered] through the provost of your basilica of holy ordination. Whatever we have given to you, or whatever we have given to each person, or what we have asked to be done, all this we beg may be done and remain by your power and holy lordship after our death. And so we give to you, holy Martin, by the page of this testament half of Griciensis, and the other half, with the buildings and with all its rights, our monks living at Attanum are to possess for ever, with you, holy Martin, defending [them]: on this condition, namely, that the monastery, which we built at the Lord's inspiration and with his help, and the monks whom God has ordained to be there through us sinners, or whom God shall order to be ordained hereafter, that is, both from freeborn men and from our slaves, which we have made over to you, lord Martin, we commend to be ordered [by you]; so that if thereafter, God forbid, anyone wishes to take away from your power what has been built for you, holy Martin, at holy places for love of Christ and in your honour and that of the saints, by any evil and wicked device, which God avert, or neglects to ordain or subject [to you] one who is held worthy to rule and govern [it], without the oversight of your holy basilica, let him be anathema through your miracles.

Our portion of the estate of Sisciacum, that is, the house and oratory with the other buildings, fields, woods, meadows, pastures and tenants [Ed., plots], with all its rights, as it is possessed by us at the present time, [we give to] your holy basilica, lord Martin, and also to the commended monks of Attanum, whom we decree to live under your patronage, so that you may have God favourable; and the slaves from that same estate of Sisciacum we have given to you, lord Martin, and to your monks, that is, to the share of your basilica, three ploughmen, Parminius, Talasius and Claudius, and also our other slaves, or whoever owe us due service, except those who are already free, namely Clara and Marcia; Ursacius with his wife and children we likewise give you into service, but on this condition, that they cultivate four arpents of vineyard each.

Our cell too, dedicated in honour of St Medard, which is seen to lie below Gaudomarum [Al., Gandomorum] and is commonly called Exidolium, with all its appurtenances, the monks of Attanum are to possess, with you, lord Martin, defending [them]. Our house of Nonniacum with buildings, vineyards, woods, meadows and pastures, and with all its rights, and likewise Luciacum [and] Marcomons, with vineyards and all their rights, as they have been possessed by us by God's favour, we wish our monks of Attanum to have through you, holy Martin, and we ask that they possess them with you defending [them], with the slaves of these names: Parminius with his wife and children, Leomeres with his wife and children, Armedius with his wife and children, Husticus with his wife and children, Claudius, Silvius with his wife and children. These likewise are to cultivate four arpents of vineyard each for the monks, and their wives are to pay ten silver pieces each every year to our aforesaid monks of Attanum, and let no one at any time presume to exact anything more from them. Their own holdings, small fields and little vineyards, they are to possess with no one disturbing [them], but on this condition, that they do not presume to sell or alienate them. Our house of Scauriniacum, which is called our portion [Al., which is due to us], apart from what we have given or what we have sold, with vineyards, meadows, woods and pastures: half your basilica, lord Martin, instituted as heir, is to take over, and half we ask with humble supplication that our monks of Attanum may have through you. Eufrasius and Meroalidus we have assigned as vinedressers of your vineyard [Al., basilica], lord Martin, on this condition, that they cultivate and tend [Al., direct] four arpents of vineyard each.

Valentinianus likewise we assign to the aforesaid monks, so that he too cultivate four arpents of vineyard for the monks, and nothing more. His wife Sufronia, and their children, if they have any, are to remain in freedom. To the basilica of the holy lord Martin we have given our portion of the estate of Rofiacum, the house named Juliacum, with all its rights. Likewise also by gift we wish Genuliacum with buildings, meadows, woods and pastures, and all its rights, to be given to St Martial. And from Scauriniacum, five arpents of cultivated vineyard, which Provincianus the vinedresser cultivated, and at Negiacum [the] arpents of cultivated vineyard, which we give as our offering, so that those serving St Martial or his register of the poor may receive them through our holy heir. The plot with our house within the walls of the city of Limoges, with its entry and exit, your basilica, holy Martin, and our monks of Attanum are to possess in equal succession. Likewise in the fort of Issaudun they are to possess with like equity the plot within the walls with our house [Al., possess (pl. imperative)].

Our portion of Eustriacum we wish to be given to Florentia and her children, and our freedmen, whose names are listed below, are to stand under your defence, holy lord Martin; that is, Castorius with his wife Limphasia, Oitardus with his wife Exsuperia, Aquilinus and Pascentius with their wives and children, Mallostes with his wife, Antedia with her son, Leotchardus with his wife Gaudiosa, Gariabandus with his wife, Faustinus with his wife Ermentaria, John with his wife and children, Marometus with his wife Sanctondia, Frontuinus with his wife and children, Antonia, Nimasius with his wife Maria, Majorianus with his wife Gerontia, Leonetus with his wife Bajola, Basulus with his wife Avencia, Mauricius with his wife Margaridia, Sanieldus with his wife Marcella, Leontius with his wife Euminia, Urretia, Eulia, whom we ransomed from captivity, Romana with her children, the children of Burgonerus, Frontasius with his children; Hildemodus with his wife and children we order to be free, with their small fields and little vineyards, and whatever holdings they have or may be able to have hereafter we wish to be granted [them], on this condition however, that they have no power to sell or give away any of the small fields or vineyards. Procula and Macedonia we likewise order to serve there, and also these slaves and their kin, listed below, we order to be [counted] our slaves: Solemius with his wife and children, Maurencianus with his wife Valeriana, Aligilius with his wife Basilia, Aliasonius with his wife Florentina, Specia with his wife Eugeria [Al., Eugenia], Lupicinus with his wife Hoctorecia with children, Francardus with his wife Orngia with children, Amaretus with his wife Savina, Frangomeres with his wife Leoboda, Partenius with his wife Mariosa, Sonulfus [Al., Ronulfus] with his wife Animia and children. We have named their kin, but we have also made some of them free: these, with their small fields and little vineyards, and whatever they are seen to have or may yet come to have, we decree they shall have, on condition that each year they bring three pounds' weight to our *carra*, and each month in turn bring blessed bread (*eulogiae*) to our masses, and bring five silver pieces to the altar, and give a gift according to what their poverty can provide: nothing more is to be required of them, either by the basilica of St Martin or by our monks, than that they must fulfil what is written.

And these our freedmen and freedwomen, whom our father Jucundus of good memory commended to us by his testament, and likewise those whom we made free for the salvation of [the soul of] our brother [Al., son] Eustadius of good memory, we commend to you, holy Martin, to be defended. And if anyone wishes to disturb or lord it over them in any way beyond what is enjoined on them, may you, holy Martin, defend [them]. And also these women, whom we have written below, that is, Baudonidis with her children, Habenda, Allovera, Fraterna, Amasonia, Artemia, Susanna, Proba, Probatia, Frotania, are to pay one *triens* (third of a gold shilling) each every year to our monks, and let no one presume to require more of them, lest he incur what is stated above. Our horses and small beasts, or cows, sheep and oxen, and pigs, bedding, household utensils, or whatever the administrator of St Martin finds in our storerooms or yards after our death, he is to give half to the poor, and our aforesaid monks are to receive the other half.

We add also the slaves who are called *colonaria* (tenant slaves) and are held to be tributary to us [Al., are owed]: half is to go to your basilica, lord Martin, and the other half is to benefit our monks, and all are to pay a *triens* each year. That is: Eulodius with his children, who are owed to us, Renchardus with his children, Friardus with his children, Amanda with her children, Gundemerus without [Ed., with] children, Dominica with her daughter. Therefore we have given the aforesaid slaves to these holy places, so that the reward for them may free us sinners.

That each holy place established there should have its service-vessels declared, we have thought right to insert: that is, four towers, three small silk covers, four silver chalices. Two are handled, bought for thirty solidi each. The middle one, worked with gold, is worth thirty solidi, and the fourth is worth thirteen solidi. A silver paten worth seventy-two solidi. Four silk covers: one is worth thirty solidi, another sixteen solidi, the third fifteen solidi, the fourth forty-five solidi. Two of them are worked with gold. Item, an ornamented linen cover worth four solidi, four corporal cloths, three silk covers, five smaller ones, and cloths, *tribunalia* [Al., *tribunae*] (hangings for the apse) in the basilica worth twelve solidi, and other daily ones worth six solidi, and other daily ones which are before the altar worth five solidi. Ornamented curtains for the main door worth three solidi. Other curtains for the same door worth three solidi. Item, a curtain for the lesser door worth two solidi. Item, a painted curtain worth five solidi. Likewise in the oratory of St Hilary a crown with a gilded silver cross with precious gems, full of relics of the holy lords, with its ornament, worth by estimate one hundred solidi, that crown having on it hanging leaves made of gold and gems, eight in number; and on that cross two made alike, and small; a large gem with gold all around, and beneath a little cross of gold, and eight little gems. A silk altar-cloth with its ornament worth twelve solidi. Item, a cloth over the little altar of St Hilary bordered with gold and worked with pearls, worth thirty solidi. Three small curtains along the walls of that oratory, ornamented with silk, worth eight solidi. Item, a daily cloth over the altar of lord Hilary, worth two solidi. Item, a curtain in [the church of] lord Hilary of *dramioserico* (half-silk?), worth forty solidi. Item, in [the church of] lord Maximinus three small curtains. Before the altar one scarlet, worth two solidi, and the other two, worth three solidi. And item, a scarlet cloth in [the church of] lord Julian, worth one solidus. A daily cloth in [the church of] lord Maximinus ornamented with silk, corporal cloths in [the church of] lord Hilary and small daily curtains for the doors. Item, for cloths over the holy tomb, two silk ones, worth sixty solidi. Item, five cloths over the tombs adorned with Achaean work, worth fifteen solidi. Item, a *profedata* [Al., *proserica*] cloth, worth two solidi. Item, another *profedata*, worth one solidus. Two curtains before those tombs, worth five solidi. All these, and the ornaments of the saints, and whatever is over our tombs of the saints of the martyrium of Attanum, we have consigned to Scipio the deacon and Aventiolus, whom we appointed to keep and tend them before the saints, and to our lord Nicetius, deacon of St Martin; together also from the oratory of Sisciacum two *tribunalia* worth four solidi, three curtains for the doors, worth six solidi; towers, chalices, cloths and covers we have handed over to the aforesaid keepers of the martyrium to keep.

And further we adjure the provost of St Martin and our monks of Attanum by the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ and the merits of all the saints, that in the oratory of St Hilary, in my cell, on Thursday, at all times, matins be celebrated rather early, and the mass of the holy lords, by the monks there. And you are to order the roofs of the saints' [churches] repaired when it is necessary, that is at Attanum and Sisciacum, admonishing the monks, and our freedmen, slaves and tenants, so that these holy places may at all times be kept up, as is the custom, namely that this be preserved as arranged just as we have left it, as is fitting in the Lord Jesus Christ. But those who are unwilling to serve us or our monastery and congregation are to be held strangers to all our property, both while we survive and after our death.

If the people of Attanum, while we live, give help, as they please, to the monks of Vosidum, we willingly give [them] our portion at Fexitoialum and one hundred arpents of land at Sisciacum; but if they refuse to give help, may you, holy Martin, recall what was given them by us to your basilica, and all things commended to you by the monks of Attanum, to be possessed forever.

Whatever is perhaps not included in this our Testament, or has been left out where it should have been put: if any bit of land or any movable thing is found, let our heir lord Martin recall all of it to be claimed for himself. If any slaves remain and are found outside the testament, both those who have produced charters of freedom and those who have none are to remain in freedom, with St Martin defending [them]. And whatever we have given by charters confirmed with the subscription of our hand, we have ordered to be wholly valid. But if anyone wishes to go against this our testament, or attempts to go otherwise than as is done here by our deliberation, let him be excommunicated and anathematized both here and in eternity by the powers of the holy and blessed lord Martin, and let that curse come upon him which Psalm 108 contains against Judas Iscariot. If any insertions or erasures are found, we made them while we reread our testament many times, and we decided to correct it.

I, ARedius, in the name of Christ a sinner and priest, wrote our testament, reread it, and signed it, on the day and year as above. I, PELAGIA, reread our testament and subscribed it on the day and year as above. I, ASTIDIUS, at the request of my lord Aredius and of Pelagia, subscribed our testament made by them. I, CALPURNUS, at the request of my lord Aredius and Pelagia, subscribed this Testament, on the day and year as above. I, LEO, asked by lord Aredius and Pelagia, confirmed this Testament, on the day and year as above. I, NECTARIUS, confirmed this Testament, at the request of lord Aredius and Pelagia.
